United States Court of Appeals
FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA CIRCUIT
____________
No. 26-5172                                                 September Term, 2025
1:26-cv-00688-RJL
Filed On: June 15, 2026
Massimiliano Cali and L.C., a minor child, by
and through her father Massimilano Cali,
Appellees
v.
Donald J. Trump, President of the United
States, et al.,
Appellants

KATSAS, Circuit Judge, concurring: This case involves the
President’s imposition of economic sanctions on a non-resident
alien based on her speech outside the United States. The
district court preliminarily enjoined the sanctions as a likely
violation of the First Amendment. Because that Amendment
does not extend to the speech of aliens abroad, I vote to stay
the injunction pending the government’s appeal.

In sum, the First Amendment claim that the plaintiffs seek
to raise on Albanese’s behalf lacks merit, and the equitable
balance favors the government. Accordingly, I vote to grant
the motion for a stay pending appeal.

US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots

The 9th Circuit Court calls the petition to remove 20,000 ballots from California’s vote count unconstitutional.

 

Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli speaks after a court hearing on October 27 over a lawsuit to set aside 20,000 ballots in California [Daniel Cole/Reuters]

By Al Jazeera Staff

Published On 30 Oct 2026

For the second time in less than a week, a United States appeals court has rejected a petition from the administration of President Donald Trump to set aside 20,000 ballots in California over concerns about non-citizen voting.

The decision came down on Friday, with less than four days until the November 3 midterm elections.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Trump’s request would violate the US Constitution and risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

“The consequence of the United States’s request is not merely ballot segregation, but ultimately both the cancellation of the ballot and the removal of voters from the voting rolls,” the majority wrote in its ruling.

Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez – appointed by Trump and his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden, respectively – formed the majority.

A third judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, issued a dissent, saying the administration’s petition was a “reasonable request”.

The Trump administration has claimed that nearly 20,000 “likely non-citizens” received mail-in ballots to vote in California’s midterm elections on November 3.

seltz.title: ACLJ Files Merits Brief at D.C. Circuit: President’s Power To Defend Israel From ICC Lawfare Is on the Line | American Center for Law and Justice
seltz.snippet:
Back in June, we told you about a major win. The D.C. Circuit stayed a district court injunction that had gutted President Trump’s sanctions against Francesca Albanese, the U.N. “Special Rapporteur” who spent years urging the International Criminal Court (ICC) to prosecute Israeli officials – including a sitting head of government. As we explained then, that stay was a significant victory for presidential authority, and the court specifically considered the ACLJ’s arguments in reaching it.

But a stay pending appeal only pauses the damage. Now the real fight begins – on the merits. The ACLJ has just filed a new amicus brief in *Cali v. Trump* at the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, and the stakes could not be higher.

Albanese herself never challenged her own sanctions designation in court. Instead, her husband and daughter did – asking a district judge not just to protect their own narrow interests, but to invalidate the Secretary of State’s entire foreign policy determination and enjoin the President’s Executive order outright. The district court agreed, and its order swept far beyond anything the law allows. Our brief lays out why that ruling cannot stand.

First, Article III doesn’t let family members borrow someone else’s grievance. Under *Department of State v. Muñoz*, downstream harm to relatives doesn’t create a constitutional right to challenge government action directed at someone else. Albanese chose not to fight her designation. Her husband and daughter can’t do it for her.

Second, even where real injuries exist, the Supreme Court’s landmark decision in *Trump v. CASA, Inc.* forbids courts from issuing relief broader than necessary to redress the actual plaintiffs’ actual harms. Nullifying an entire national security designation to fix a licensing dispute is like demolishing a house to patch a leaky faucet.

The D.C. Circuit, including Robert Bork (blocked from confirmation by liberal senators), Clarence Thomas, John Roberts, and Brett Kavanaugh.

Under longstanding court rules, a decision by this (and all other U.S. Courts of Appeals) is not final until a petition for rehearing en banc, if filed, is decided. KATSAS, Circuit Judge, concurring: This case involves the
President’s imposition of economic sanctions on a non-resident
alien based on her speech outside the United States. The
district court preliminarily enjoined the sanctions as a likely
violation of the First Amendment. Because that Amendment
does not extend to the speech of aliens abroad, I vote to stay
the injunction pending the government’s appeal.

In sum, the First Amendment claim that the plaintiffs seek
to raise on Albanese’s behalf lacks merit, and the equitable
balance favors the government. Accordingly, I vote to grant
the motion for a stay pending appeal.
